newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN PREMIER WINS NARROW PARTY BACKING.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN PREMIER WINS NARROW PARTY BACKING.

text.p: Bulgaria's Prime Minister Zhan Videnov on Tuesday won a confidence vote from his party by a narrow margin, giving him backing to stay in office and to seek introduction of IMF-proposed currency control measures.
A total of 87 members of the party's supreme council voted to support the premier at the end of a marathon 20-hour meeting, 69 voted against him and two abstained.
The meeting made no cabinet changes and Videnov said any reshuffle would be discussed at a full party congress scheduled for December 21 and 22.

Three members of the executive bureau resigned, including party vice chairman Yanaki Stoilov. Influential former party chairman Alexander Lilov said their departure would fuel opposition pressure for early parliamentary elections.
"I expect the opposition to start to carry out its intentions," Lilov told reporters.

Stoilov and Lilov were among 19 party members who signed a letter last week calling for a new cabinet and wide-ranging policy reforms. Speakers on Monday and Tuesday called for a new cabinet with new policies but put forward no names.
About 20 elderly Socialists outside the party headquarters denounced pro-reform delegates as traitors and renegades as they left the meeting. They surrounded Lilov, asking: "How could you do this?"
The Bulgarian Socialist Party is made up mainly of ex-communists who renamed their party after former leader Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989.

Videnov told the plenum he supported introduction of a currency board proposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to restore confidence in the collapsing lev, and asked the party for backing to start negotiations.
The measure must be approved by parliament, where the Socialists are half way through their four-year term.
Under the currency board system, the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves.
The system, which pegs the local currency usually to the dollar, has been used by Argentina, Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation.

Michael Deppler, deputy director of the IMF's European department, left Sofia on Tuesday. An IMF statement described his talks as "very useful" and said they would be followed by technical missions to discuss details of the currency board.

"With this preparatory work, the necessary public support, and agreement on a strong policy package, an arrangement with the Fund around the turn of the year is a realistic objective," the statement said.

The IMF has twice postponed a badly-needed $115 million credit due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets. Agreement with the Fund is vital if the Balkan state is to avoid defaulting on its $10 billion foreign debt.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development on Tuesday warned Bulgaria to stick to its reform plans if it wanted more of its support, singling out lack of corporate governance and corruption as holding up progress.
Bulgaria has the lowest levels of foreign investment in the region and gross domestic product is scheduled to shrink by up to 10.5 percent this year.
Main trade unions are discussing plans for a one-day general strike to protest against falling living standards.
The lev has collapsed from 70 to the dollar in January to 256 on Tuesday and annual inflation is forecast at 240 percent.
